podcast.title: Bowie's Return to Band Format (1988)
podcast.body: Formed in 1988, Tin Machine marked David Bowie's first time being in a band since the early 1960s, representing a deliberate shift towards a more collaborative and hard-edged sound driven by his personal musical preferences. "It was the first time that Bowie had been in a band since sometime in the early 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's "Roots" Return (1989)
podcast.body: The band was marketed as David Bowie returning to his roots as the frontman of a small rock combo, akin to his earlier days leading bands like the Manish Boys or the Lower Third. This was a deliberate move to submerge his pop identity into a grungy rock sound. "The band was billed as Bowie returning to his roots as the frontman of a small rock combo, like his 60s days leading the Manish Boys or the lower third."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Failure to Develop Identity (1989-1992)
podcast.body: Despite proving decent radio fodder, Tin Machine never developed a personality beyond its status as "David Bowie's side project." This, coupled with poor album sales (their debut didn't even go gold, and "Tin Machine II" reached a meager number 126), ultimately led Bowie to return to his solo career after a three-year experiment. "While Tin Machine's workmen like Alt Rock proved decent radio fodder, the band never developed a personality beyond its status as David Bowie's side project."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Ahead of Its Time
podcast.body: Bowie had correctly anticipated that music would become heavier and angrier, but Tin Machine's fundamental problem was that they were "doing that two or three years before the world was ready for it," suggesting a re-evaluation of their historical significance is needed. "Bowie had correctly ascertained that music was going to get heavier and angrier. Tin Machine's problem is that they were doing that two or three years before the world was ready for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alternative/College Chart Success (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Tin Machine's timing was opportune for the nascent modern rock chart, launched by Billboard a year prior, which tracked airplay on alternative and college stations. The band performed quite well on this chart, with multiple singles reaching the top 11. "Bowie's timing was good in at least one way. The year before, Billboard had launched a new modern rock chart to track airplay on alternative and college stations, and Tin Machine did quite well on that chart."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Anticipation of Grunge
podcast.body: It has been argued that Tin Machine's sound notably pre-saged the Grunge movement that emerged a couple of years later, making them a "visionary" group in retrospect for their influence on 90s rock and alternative music. "But I've argued that Tin Machine pre-saged Grunge a couple of years later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's 90s Reinvention
podcast.body: Tin Machine was formed by David Bowie as part of his 90s reinvention, envisioned as a four-piece rock band with Bowie as the lead singer, drawing inspiration from artists like Jimi Hendrix, Cream, and The Pixies. Their debut record had a distinct sound, not easily mistaken for a typical David Bowie release. "His idea was to form a four-piece rock band with him as the lead singer. Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream, and the Pixies. They called themselves Tin Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fan and Critic Backlash
podcast.body: Despite initial success, the band "soon ran out of steam" as fans and critics felt that Bowie had "stopped being Bowie," leading to a lack of fond remembrance for the project among many of his followers. "Fans and critics felt that Bowie had stopped being Bowie. There was a second album and a live record, and then the band broke up in 1992. Tin Machine is frankly not remembered fondly by many Bowie fans, if at all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Formation as a Four-Piece Rock Band
podcast.body: David Bowie formed Tin Machine with the explicit idea of creating a four-piece rock band where he would serve solely as the lead singer. This project was a conscious effort to flush away the baggage of his past hits and artistic personas, drawing inspiration from the raw aesthetics of bands like Jimi Hendrix, Cream, and the Pixies. "His idea was to form a four piece rock band with him just as the lead singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Harsh Critical Reception
podcast.body: The two albums released by Tin Machine between 1989 and 1991 received very harsh reviews. Critics often judged the band not only against David Bowie's celebrated past works but also against the rising tide of alternative music at the time, perceiving Bowie as an "old man trying to be hip again" with his rock band. "There would be two Tin Machine albums before the project was retired and during this time which would be between 1989 and 1991, they received some pretty harsh reviews."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hypothetical Success in Later Years
podcast.body: It is proposed that if Tin Machine had emerged later, "in, let's say 1992 or 1993," their reception and impact "would have been very, very different," implying that their timing was their primary impediment to greater success. "I think Tin Machine requires a re-evaluation. If they had arrived in, let’s say 1992 or 1993, I maintained that things would have been very, very different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Initial Muted Reception, Later Re-evaluation
podcast.body: Upon their first record's release, Tin Machine received a "muted" reaction from critics and fans. However, the project has since been favorably re-evaluated, recognized as "visionary" for its prescient sound that pre-saged the grunge, rock, and alternative music movements of the 1990s. "Reaction was... muted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predating 1990s Hard Rock
podcast.body: Tin Machine's experimental and very hard sound significantly predated much of the grunge, punk, and hardcore music that would become prevalent in the 1990s, showcasing Bowie's accurate foresight into the future direction of rock music. "Tin Machine was experimental and very hard, predating a lot of the music that we would hear with Grunge and Punk and Hardcore in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Charismatic Interview Subject (1990, Tin Machine era)
xref.body: In 1990, during his Tin Machine years, David Bowie exhibited a profound level of charisma in an interview, similar to Bono. He maintained intense eye contact, creating an immersive experience for the interviewer, who was so overwhelmed that they forgot to record the conversation. Years later, when reminded of the incident, Bowie directly yet humorously acknowledged the error. "The only other person with that level of charisma that I ever talked to was David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lost Interview Tape (1990)
xref.body: In 1990, prior to the ongoing history show, the speaker had a 30-minute, face-to-face interview with David Bowie during his Tin Machine years. The speaker was so overwhelmed by Bowie's presence, focusing on his various personas, that he forgot to unpause his tape machine, resulting in no recording. "And I don't remember what I asked him. I don't remember what he said because I was just like, this is Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

Bowie's idea was to form a four-piece rock band with himself purely as the lead singer, drawing on the raw energy and format of such influential artists. "Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream and the Pixies."

Bowie aimed to create a four-piece rock band with himself solely as the lead singer, harkening back to the dynamic and influential styles of bands like Cream. xref.title: Inspiration for Tin Machine
xref.body: The Pixies were cited as an inspiration for David Bowie's band Tin Machine. Bowie's vision for Tin Machine was a four-piece rock band where he would primarily serve as the lead singer, drawing inspiration from the raw, impactful sound of bands like the Pixies. "Inspiration was taken from Jimmy Hendrix, Cream and the Pixies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Tin Machine Return to Solo Career
xref.body: After Tin Machine broke up in 1992, David Bowie reverted to his solo identity, achieving "decent success," though not on the same scale as his iconic 1970s and early 1980s period. "After Tin Machine broke up in 1992, David Bowie went back to being, well, David Bowie. He had some decent success, but nothing like what we saw in the 70s and early 80s."
